Chapter 9: Trusting the Unseen and the Power of Faith.
Have you ever found yourself staring into the unknown, where every step forward feels like you're walking through a thick fog? For anyone who's ever tried to create something new, you know that feeling. It's both scary and strangely necessary. It’s those moments that call for a special kind of faith—a belief in things you can’t see or prove.
Imagine standing at a crossroads, not sure which path to take. There are options everywhere, and every direction comes with its own risks. There’s no guarantee you’ll succeed, no way to predict if you’ll be safe. All you have is that quiet inner voice, nudging you toward what feels right. Most of us want to wait for certainty, don’t we? But those who create—artists, dreamers, and thinkers—learn to move forward anyway. They lean into the process, even when the outcome is hidden.
It’s completely normal to want proof before you leap. Who doesn’t want some reassurance that their hard work will actually pay off? But creativity doesn’t play by those rules. Instead, it asks you to trust—to take risks, to stumble and sometimes fall, and to keep going even when the way ahead is dark.
Think about those moments of doubt everyone faces. Maybe it's a big setback, a harsh rejection, or a project that just doesn't work out. The easy move is to give up, to run back to what's safe. But what if, instead, you kept going? What if you trusted that your work had meaning, even if no one else could see it yet? Sometimes, believing in your own experience—no matter how hard it is to explain—makes all the difference.
That kind of trust isn’t loud or flashy. It grows quietly, step by step, until it becomes a real strength. You start to rely on your own instincts, listening to the wisdom that bubbles up from inside. You realize that faith isn’t about being certain—it’s about having the courage to act, even when you’re filled with doubt.
Here’s something worth remembering: the biggest breakthroughs often come when you have no idea what’s going to happen next. The work that matters most usually feels the riskiest. So, the real challenge? It’s to keep moving forward, to believe in the journey itself, even if you can’t see where it ends.
